title: Simple-reflection length counts positive roots sent negative
statement: Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real vector space [def-weil-vector-space-dimension] with a positive definite symmetric bilinear form $(\ ,\ )$. Let $\Phi\subseteq V\setminus\{0\}$ be finite and span $V$, and suppose that $\Phi\cap\mathbf R\alpha=\{\alpha,-\alpha\}$ for each $\alpha\in\Phi$, that $s_\alpha(v)=v-2(v,\alpha)(\alpha,\alpha)^{-1}\alpha$ permutes $\Phi$, and that $2(\beta,\alpha)/(\alpha,\alpha)\in\mathbf Z$ for all roots $\alpha,\beta$. Let $\Delta\subseteq\Phi$ be a real vector-space basis such that each root has integer $\Delta$-coordinates all nonnegative or all nonpositive. Put $\Phi^+=\{\beta\in\Phi:\text{all its }\Delta\text{-coordinates are nonnegative}\}$. Let $W_\Delta$ be the subgroup of $\operatorname{GL}_{\mathbf R}(V)$ generated by $\{s_\alpha:\alpha\in\Delta\}$. For $w\in W_\Delta$, let $\ell(w)$ be the least number of simple reflections in an expression for $w$, and call such a minimal expression reduced. Then for every $w\in W_\Delta$, $$\ell(w)=\#\{\beta\in\Phi^+:w\beta\in-\Phi^+\}.$$ When $V=0$, both sides are zero for the unique element of $W_\Delta=\{1\}$.

source.place: Proposition 4.4.4, printed pp.102--104 (PDF pp.110--112), and Lemma 4.4.3; finite crystallographic real-reflection formulation as in Milne iAG2017 Appendix C.8--C.11, printed pp.609--610. Brion--Kumar Section 2.1 equation (1), printed p.61, gives the same count. Local Björner--Brenti PDF WANTED; university-hosted text read online.

proof.text: Put $P=\Phi^+$ and $I(v)=\{\beta\in P:v\beta\in-P\}$. Nonzero roots have a nonzero coordinate, so the coordinate-sign hypothesis and $-\Phi=\Phi$ give $\Phi=P\sqcup(-P)$. For $a\in\Delta$, substitution in the reflection formula gives $s_a a=-a$, $(s_a x,a)=-(x,a)$ and $s_a^2x=x$. Thus inverse simple reflections equal themselves; finite products of them form the generated subgroup, and the nonempty set of word lengths for each $w\in W_\Delta$ has a least member. Products act with the rightmost reflection first.

source.place: Appendix C.8--C.11, printed pp.609--610; elementary consequences of the explicit reflection and base definitions.

proof.text: Fix $a\in\Delta$ and $\beta\in P\setminus\{a\}$. Reducedness $\Phi\cap\mathbf R a=\{a,-a\}$ shows that some coordinate of $\beta$ at a different simple root is positive. The formula for $s_a\beta$ changes only its $a$-coordinate. It is a root with that other coordinate still positive, so all its coordinates are nonnegative. It cannot equal $a$, since applying $s_a$ would give $\beta=-a$. Hence $s_a$ maps $P\setminus\{a\}$ into itself; its involutivity gives equality. This verifies the sign-preservation hypothesis of the deletion lemma with $R=\Phi$, $D=\Delta$.

source.place: Lemma 4.4.3, printed p.102 (PDF p.110); direct coordinate argument for the present unnormalized roots.

proof.text: Induct on $n=\ell(w)$, simultaneously for all $w$. For $n=0$, $w=1$ and $I(w)=\varnothing$. For $n>0$, choose a reduced expression $w=s_{a_1}\cdots s_{a_n}=u s_a$ with $a=a_n$. Its prefix $u$ has length $n-1$, since replacing it by a shorter word would shorten $w$. If $ua\in-P$, apply [lem-sfb-root-sign-word-deletion] to the prefix word and $b=a\in P$: steps 1--2 verify every hypothesis. The lemma forces $n-1\geq1$ and expresses $u s_a=w$ by deleting a letter from that prefix, a word of length $n-2$, contradicting reducedness. Therefore $ua\in P$, since $u$ permutes $\Phi$.

source.place: Proposition 4.4.4, printed pp.102--104; the required simple-root sign criterion is obtained from the existing sign-word deletion lemma, rather than assuming a Coxeter presentation.

proof.text: For this $w=u s_a$, one has $a\notin I(u)$ and $w a=-ua\in-P$, so $a\in I(w)$. For $\beta\in P\setminus\{a\}$, step 2 gives $s_a\beta\in P\setminus\{a\}$, and $\beta\in I(w)$ is equivalent to $s_a\beta\in I(u)$. Applying the same involution to this equivalence yields the disjoint union $$I(w)=s_a(I(u))\sqcup\{a\}.$$ Since $s_a$ is bijective and $P$ is finite, $\#I(w)=\#I(u)+1$. The induction hypothesis gives $\#I(u)=n-1$, hence $\#I(w)=n=\ell(w)$.

source.place: Proposition 4.4.4, printed p.104 (PDF p.112); explicit finite-set bijection and induction step.

proof.text: If $V=0$, the condition $\Phi\subseteq V\setminus\{0\}$ forces $\Phi=\Delta=P=\varnothing$. The generated subgroup contains only the empty product $1$, whose least word length and inversion count are both zero. Thus the same argument includes the stated degenerate case.

source.place: Appendix C.8--C.11; empty-root and empty-word case supplied explicitly.
